t: The Problem With Perfectionism
q: The difference between aiming for perfection and demanding it is a chasm leaders must come to terms with.
Leaders and performers who demand perfectionism are guaranteed to be continually disappointed.
Perfectionism is a curse that leaders and performers too often apply on purpose.
Research for more than a century reveals that over time, perfectionists are less successful than non-perfectionists at just about everything.
Winston Churchill almost perfectly described the effects of perfectionism in just three words: “Perfectionism spells paralysis.

t: Leaders Who Hide Behind Their Intentions Dont Apologize Often Enough
q: Too many leaders hide behind their intentions and fail to apologize for their misdeeds.
Many leaders view mistakes and the apologies that follow them as signs of weakness.
Simply believing that they didn’t intend to do harm, insult, or offense doesn’t allow a leader to explain away the transgression.
By admitting to and taking full ownership of your mistakes, you show yourself to be human, not weak.
The symbolism of saying you’re sorry goes well beyond the present moment. It is a powerful reflection of how a leader relates to the truth.

t: The Bell is My Boss, Too
q: None of you wants to hear an adult haranguing you each day to start class; that's unpleasant for you and it's unpleasant for me. That's a terrible way to start our time together. Because of that, we'll let the bell be our boss.
Yes — that is what that means. If I've not completed the lesson by the time the bell rings, that's my error and something I need to work on. You've got another class to get to in only five minutes.
I want to be the most gently efficient and competent teacher that I can be, and so I need that closing bell to mean that my class is over.

Otherwise, I'll get loosey-goosey with class endings and class middles and class beginnings. When the bell cuts me short, I want to be cut short, and I want to learn from the experience of having not finished the lesson.

And sure, telling my students that the bell is OUR boss, not just theirs — that does help with my Credibility by signaling that I'm fair. But that's not the most important reason to use the bell this way.
The most important reason is that using the bell this way makes us better.

t: How To Plan For A Sub And Ensure Good Behavior
q: You must have at least one solid substitute teacher on speed dial and preferably a couple of backups you trust will follow your plan and schedule precisely.
Never lighten the load because you have a sub. This sends the message to your students that the day doesn’t matter, which causes silliness, misbehavior, and a whole day of lost learning.
You must choose a sub who understands the critical importance of following your classroom management plan, daily schedule, and routines to the letter.
If you follow the SCM approach, then having a substitute teacher is easy because they can follow your plan as clearly and unemotionally as you.
The good news is that the most sought-after subs will love coming to your classroom because they get to actually teach instead of babysit.

t: Motivation: The Cause of Doing Work or the Effect?
q: Is motivation the CAUSE of doing the work of learning or the EFFECT? As it turns out, it's both.
Does this teacher actually care about me? Does he know what he's doing? Is his passion real? (These are Credibility questions.)
The Five Key Beliefs of student motivation aren't just a cause of doing work, they're also an effect.

When my children were younger, no amount of mini-sermonizing or MGCing could have convinced them that they were swimmers. What they needed was clear, brief instruction on basic swimming sub-skills and then immediate, in-the-water, no-opt-out practice.
It was the actual swimming that quickly changed their sense of identification with the act.
And so, paradoxically, motivation is both the cause AND the effect of doing work.

t: Introducing the Provocative Challenge
q: Bound to a false belief or opinion, or a behavior with unintended consequences, people sometimes need a bolt of lightning to set them on a different course.
It is essential to remember that what makes the message provocative is not the way it is delivered but the surprise it contains relative to current awareness.
To avoid the possible negative reactions of others, good leaders devise a way of introducing a challenge that makes the provocation less threatening and easier to accept.
Keeping the assertion high while lowering the confidence from which it is offered can do wonders for the acceptance of the challenge.
In its best form, it always holds the relationship equal to the message. That’s why the challenge is worth presenting in the first place.

t: Leaders Who Dont Suffer Fools Gladly
q: Leaders who don’t suffer fools gladly, as the expression goes, have a difficult time tolerating incompetence or sloppy thinking.
While this reputation has some advantages, it is generally not the compliment leaders secretly think it is.

When leaders treat people dismissively, for the perception of adding too little to the discussion, they create a chilling effect on everyone’s willingness to take conversational risks and express ideas openly.
They rightly believe a leader who lets it be known through their actions and comments that they perceive a fool in their midst likely doesn’t care about people’s feelings.
As it turns out, leaders who don’t suffer fools gladly look profoundly foolish in the eyes of others.

q: But dishonesty, no matter how shaded or nuanced, not only destroys your best strategies, but it guarantees that your students
One boy was knocked unconscious and left in the street. He died two days later.
Would the bully who, according to witnesses, danced on the body of the boy who died have made a different choice that night if he had been given
It plants a seed that develops ruthlessness devoid of fault or responsibility and manipulation that feigns remorse and garners sympathy.
Now one boy is dead and six others are facing life in prison. The road to hell is paved with good intentions indeed.

t: Five First Week Reflections
q: But here's one thing I know: 134 is a lot of human beings to get to know in a week! Especially for an introverted guy like me.

When you read things they've written, picture their face as best you can. Find those connection points — the quicker you can attach meaning to their name and face, the quicker you'll gain a sense of knowing them as humans and not just as 134 people to get to know.
I needed to bring my A-game with mini-sermons because I knew they were. And I knew a bunch of other folks all around the country were doing it.
This serves the obvious benefit of giving me insight into the hearts of my students, though a real but invisible side benefit is that this cultivates the Belonging belief, too.

Everest Statements, like all the tools I recommend, are only as useful as we make them. And each time we practice communicating Everest, our skill improves, as does the likelihood that the Everest will sink in.
It's because of you that I've written my books, that I've travelled to a dozen or so schools this past summer, and continue to push forward my practice in the simple yet deep areas I write about.

t: Dont Empower the Wrong People
q: Given the many benefits of empowering others, the downside of this practice is not talked about much.
Empowering people who are not ready for it is a recipe for frustration, dissatisfaction, and disappointment for everyone involved.
Their inexperience almost guarantees failure or mishap. The assignment isn’t a stretch, but a bear trap of misfortune given their lack of skills and inexperience.
The team member has a deep need to please people more than to create great outcomes.
The best leaders empower others when they are ready or near ready for it, and not a moment before.

t: The Value Belief
q: For a human to be optimally motivated in an endeavor, they need a core question answered: does this work actually matter? Unfortunately, the average secondary student answers this with a simple "no.
First, they don't work all that well, especially when we make utility arguments about the future: People discount the value of temporally distant rewards to an extreme and irrational degree.
The biggest problem I see in teachers who rely too much on relevance is that they presume that student interests are more homogenous than they actually are.
My point is to critique the popular narrative amongst American educators that relevant curricula are a simple and self-evident good.

The more conceptions they had, the better they tended to do in school. I don't know why that is, but my guess is that a student with such a broad array of outlooks has an easier time engaging with any learning task they're presented with.
The main thing that I find helps is that I keep my grading system as simple as possible.
Overall, the most powerful thing we can do to help students who are obsessed with grades is speak to the truth that our goal is mastery, not grades.

t: Take the Expenses Quiz
q: What it costs to run a business or enterprise of any size is typically lost on people.
A best practice to accomplish a deeper appreciation of expenses and to encourage team members to more fully grasp what it takes to operate the enterprise is to make a game out of the exercise.
The idea is to surprise people with questions and answers that will give them a more considered view.
Most teams delight in trying to guess the costs involved and become fully engaged in the quiz.
When people understand the expense side of the enterprise, they are better equipped to make decisions like they own the place.

t: The Fabulous Discomfort of Exit Interviews
q: When they conduct Exit Interviews with team members who leave the team for whatever reason, the best organizations garner a wealth of valuable information about how to improve.
Exit Interviews and the data they provide are typically dreaded by the leaders who manage the departing colleague.
But, even in upset, the criticisms of those who leave usually contain kernels of truth that are worth acting on.
Did you feel as if your team leader invested in you and supported your success?
Exit Interviews are a best practice for an important reason. The best leaders want to know why people really left and what they can possibly do about it.

t: The Danger of Yes People
q: When asked point-blank what they think, a yes-person normally tells a leader what they want to hear.
But below the surface lies deception. No colleague ever says, “I’m about to tell you what you want to hear and agree with you when I don’t.
Leaders who are surrounded by yes-people are in danger of only seeing issues and problems from one point of view.
Leaders surrounded by yes-people might as well test all of their opinions in the mirror.
They recognize that tolerating yes-people leads to calamity and they want no part of it, no matter how comfortable it might feel.

t: Building Culture: How to Shape Character Through Daily Interactions https://bunsenblue.com/2024/08/20/building-culture-how-to-shape-character-through-daily-interactions/
q: I want the pupils in my classroom to become better people each day. This happens when they actually behave in a way that reflects the values we share: integrity, taking responsibility for our actions, thinking about our duty to others, working hard, being grateful, radiating positivity.

To actually invest the time and effort in helping pupils to live those values in every interaction is the tough part. But that is the very thing that will transform culture and forge character in our pupils.

If you can forge an identity where living the values you share is something worth celebrating and worthy of admiration, and explain that being in this class or school means showing integrity, then you allow others in the group a chance to belong
I so often hear teachers narrating behaviours they like to see in utilitarian ways: if you work hard, you will be able to get great qualifications and get the job you want.
I think the phrase 'manage behaviour' sets us up to view our jobs with the paradigm of getting pupils to comply with rules.
If we can make it clear to pupils what those precise actions are and reinforce them continually, through every interaction we have with them, then we can start to build a culture of excellence.

t: The Best Place and Time to Have That Conversation
q: Where a conversation takes place and what else the parties are doing during the exchange really matters.
Leaders who want to learn more about what others really think select the time, location, and activity that primes the pump for open communication.
Conversations when walking or driving seem more casual and informal because both parties are side-by-side rather than face-on.
This expectation encourages disclosure and diminishes the natural urge to pre-think or prepare to respond as they do in a more formal setting.
The best leaders don’t conduct all of their conversations from behind a desk or in a conference room.

t: Moments of Genuine Connection (MGCs) https://davestuartjr.com/tracking-attempted-moments-of-genuine-connection-mgc-dsjr-one-stop-shop-2
q: A moment of genuine connection (MGC) is simple: 30 to 60 seconds in which I, as the teacher, attempt to communicate to a student that I value, know, and/or respect them.
Because I cannot possibly mentally keep track of attempting MGCs with 100+ students each semester, I keep track of these on a printed out roster that I keep on a clipboard.

If I only connect with them as a person, they may come to believe that I'm a caring person but not a capable teacher. If I only connect with them as a learner, they may come to believe that I only care about their work in my class and not about them as a person overall.
First, like every worthwhile teaching strategy, MGC attempts are a practicable, improvable skill. There are weak MGC attempts and strong MGC attempts.

More importantly, you have to view tracking attempted MGCs as a strategy akin to long-term investing. With each series you complete, the likelihood of a student receiving the valued/respected/known signal into their heart increases.
Questions posed with curiosity and eye contact are a fine method for indicating to someone that you value them, that you want to know them, and that you respect them.

t: True Mastery Requires a Beginners Mind
q: Kano knew that death, like true mastery, makes everyone a novice all over again.
Maslow called this quality a “second naivete,” in reference to the fact that everyone is born naïve and returns to that state as they reach the highest level of psychological development.
Masters explore the fundamentals of high performance with extreme humility, believing that new insights arrive through naïve questions and inquiry.
It requires the “student” to free themselves of worry about external judgments and to operate openly without fear of being seen as a fool.
Rare are the leaders and performers willing to embrace the beginner’s mindset and admit to themselves and the world that they know very little.

t: Will You Be Bitter or Better
q: Will they choose to allow this event to make them “bitter or better?” as motivational speaker Josh Shipp likes to say.
Rather, it is about choosing how much negative control we allow the situation to have.
Those who surrender themselves to the disappointment quickly become victims of their own demise.
At the moment bitterness begins to take hold, people need the help of leaders to make a different decision.
Good leaders go out of their way to remind us that better is more powerful than bitter in tough situations.

t: Asking and Answering Your Own Questions
q: The best leaders are highly aware of the markers or cues of confidence that they use to project self-assurance.
Too many cues deployed too quickly can transform a confident leader into one viewed as arrogant or condescending.
One marker or cue worthy of examination is the device of asking and answering one’s own questions.
Overusing any marker of confidence produces a “Titanic effect” where others are more likely to view you as arrogant or full of hubris.
Becoming more aware and intentional about how you project confidence is critically important for developing a style that works best.

t: The Unexpected Ways Great Companies Show They Care About Their People
q: Some organizational rewards carry more weight because they are both unexpected and special.
The key is to do something unexpected that team members would be unlikely to do for themselves.
In fact, if team members don’t take and share photos of the reward, it probably wasn’t all that special.
This list of possible rewards is only limited by creativity.
Leaders don’t do it to create pride, to build team spirit, or to be recognized for their creativity. They do it because they care.

t: Teacher Credibility
q: Teachers are like cell phone towers. A cell tower is always sending signals, whether my cell phone is on or off. That is the cell tower's job.
In terms of Credibility, I am always sending signals to my students, whether I want to or not.
In the largest meta-analytical research effort ever undertaken in education, researcher John Hattie finds that Teacher Credibility has a massive effect size.
I do not recommend trying to convince your students that you are Credible. Instead, show them you are Credible by consistently signaling Care, Competence, and Passion.
So do some extra research, particularly outside of intra-disciplinary echo chambers, before you set your professional views in stone. It'll make the job a lot more fun and interesting.
In other words, while it's true that first days have special characteristics in the hearts of our students, it's mostly in the humdrum where Credibility is made or lost.

t: 3 Leadership Traits Every Teacher Needs
q: They tend to have an external locus of control and difficulty grasping that they alone can create the teaching experience they want.
Locus of control, whether internal or external, isn’t so much who you are, but rather a decision you make.
Not only will SCM work as it should, but your presence, confidence, boldness, and courage will grow naturally and without effort.
With SCM—or any success method regardless of endeavor—you have to perform. There is no way around it. The good news is that anyone can do it.
I’ve been told that my classroom management confidence borders on the absurd. But it’s not inborn.

t: Retaining Franchise Talent Presumes You Know Who They Are
q: In any organization, a small group of contributors makes an oversized difference in getting things done and achieving results.
Even in large organizations, the number of franchise players is rarely more than 25.
Good leaders know exactly who the franchise players are. They think about them often and do everything in their power to keep them engaged and satisfied.
Retaining the franchise players is among the most important facets of great leadership.
No need to label or tell these team members how priceless they are. The key is to show them.

t: The Five Key Beliefs Beneath Student Motivation
q: Credibility, Value, Effort, Efficacy, and Belonging — these are the roots of student motivation, which presents itself as care-driven, learning-conducive behaviors.
The Five Key Beliefs pave the path to the head. Because the path to the head, it turns out, is through the heart.

What I always tell teachers who are getting started is focus on Credibility. It's especially malleable, it's the most within your control, and it's the point of best leverage from which to influence the other beliefs.
How we shape the school or classroom context is enormously predictive of the degree to which students will pursue mastery with care. And we shape that context every day, during every encounter.
This means that comments like so-and-so is just an unmotivated student aren't accurate or helpful because they disempower the teacher to do the kinds of things that influence student motivation.
In the subsequent draft, I took the initial list of 55 strategies and reduced it to just 10.

t: Only the Mediocre Are Always at Their Best
q: French novelist Jean Giraudoux gave us that gem more than 80 years ago.
Savvy leaders come to understand that being mediocre has a host of advantages that are highly attractive to some team members.
The work-life balance of mediocre performers is usually quite good. And they like it that way.
Top-performing team members quickly come to disrespect colleagues who have no desire to improve.
Mediocrity is a virus best treated with unflinchingly high standards applied consistently.

t: Become a Better Listener and Gain Clarity With Say More
q: Active listening requires leaders to slow down and process what they hear before responding.
Having to think of a clarifying question while listening interrupts a leader’s processing and sense-making of what is being said.
Examine great listeners, those who make others truly feel heard, and you will find a simple and effective behavior that is present in almost every exchange.
Interestingly, asking others to elaborate further on what they have already said will often result in a more succinct restatement of their comments.
As several authors like to say, the best leaders learn to listen by listening to learn.

t: The Many Ways of Being Heard
q: Team members who play it safe by keeping their opinions about issues more closely guarded run the chance of not being heard and therefore not being seen as fully engaged in meetings.
Because many team members presume they must advocate or express an opinion to be heard, they sit silently when they don’t have anything special or substantive to say.
This short list is not exhaustive, nor will every tactic be appropriate in some meetings.
As a rule of thumb, a highly engaged team member should be heard every 10-15 minutes at a minimum.
Being heard is essential. The only question is when and how not if.

t: Good Apples in a Bad Barrel
q: Research over decades has confirmed that good apples placed in a bad barrel will turn sour.
Their positive qualities of fairness, empathy, objectivity and compassion encourage them to listen more attentively than perhaps they should.

More than 50 years ago, Stanford professor Philip Zimbardo proved in a series of controversial experiments that people are likely to conform to the social influence of peers even when their viewpoints go against their personal experience.
But when one or more team members go negative and lodge complaints and criticisms to negatively influence others, leaders must act swiftly to curtail the virus that is likely to spread.
Waiting and hoping for the best is how good teams turn sour.

t: Pushing Against a Candidates Flaw
q: Occasionally, a job candidate with huge upside displays a glaring flaw that prohibits their selection.
But before giving up on a promising candidate with a fatal flaw, it would be wise to first push against the blemish and see what the team can learn.
The ensuing conversation will expose how self-aware the candidate is, why they engaged the team leader in that way, and what they typically do to offset such a defect.
Candidates who are in denial of the perceptions others form or get defensive about how they presented themselves confirm that they are not a good fit.
Teams that make their thinking explicit with candidates act as leaders, offering hugely valuable feedback to someone who clearly needs it.

t: This School Year, Try the Minimalist Approach to Student Motivation
q: What I've found is that even the short list of 10 strategies I write about can be pretty overwhelming. It's too much to focus on at any given time.
Improve at One Thing – This can go because, by getting rid of it, we'll actually be doing it. By giving ourselves fewer strategies to focus on, we can get better at each one faster.
But the reason I didn't is because, by removing the three that I did, you get efficiency and focus gains that exceed the simple three strategy reduction.

Mini-sermons are simple, brief, repeated attempts to creatively and confidently explain to your students why they're doing the work they're doing. These enhance Credibility and Value with as little effort as possible.
So, I went from 10 to 7. Not much of a reduction, right? It seemed like that to me at first. I was frustrated.
So this school year, my recommendation is to play with just these seven tools as you seek to do something productive about student motivation problems in your setting.

t: Leaders and Organizations Cant Win When They Speak Out on Political Issues
q: Leaders and organizations who speak out publicly on political and social issues soon learn the controversy they most need to address is about themselves.
When leaders take a stance and attempt to do the “right” thing about issues unconnected to the core mission of the organization, everyone loses —especially the leader.
This chilling effect on openness undermines the collaborative spirit between team members that all organizations need to perform.
The best leaders refrain from taking any position or making any statement that doesn’t directly connect to its core mission.
No leadership team can or should speak for the entire audience of customers, team members, and investors.

t: How To Handle Misbehavior The First Weeks Of School
q: They’re testing you. They want to know if you’re the real deal or just like all the rest.
Most teachers will panic and jump ship in the face of even semi-aggressive push-back.
One by one, as long as you remain calm and unmovable, your students will leap as if from a burning building onto your side.
They’ve been flattered and manipulated and told in not so many words that they’re weirdly different and don’t have the ability to control themselves.
But only if you persevere undaunted. Chicken out, give in, and be another spineless pushover and you’ll never know what they’re capable of.

t: Preventing Initiative Fatigue
q: They can experience what is known as initiative fatigue, a weariness that robs them of their desire to perform.
Leaders who inadvertently burn out their teams generally do not have too many initiatives. They have too many priorities.
When leaders make every initiative a high priority, fatigue is soon to follow.
Fatigue and burnout are the result of too many priorities, not too many initiatives.
If you can’t count the most important initiatives on one hand, you’re setting the team up for fatigue and eventual failure.

t: The Complete Guide to Pop-Up Debates
q: Every student must speak at least one time. Students may not speak more than twice, unless the teacher indicates otherwise. To speak, students simply stand up (pop up) at their seats.
In the technical and competitive senses, my Pop-Up Debates are not debates. They are argument-laden discussions where students bring evidence, logic, and reasoning to the prompt at hand.

Anxiety around public speaking often makes you feel like you are the only one who's nervous. But the reality is, you're not. We'll keep working on this so you can gain comfort and confidence as the school year progresses.
The absolute best feedback I can provide my students as public speakers is letting them see themselves on video.

I often tell students that the greatest sign of respect you can receive in a Pop-Up Debate is when someone argues with what you've said. This means that they were listening and that they've taken your words seriously.
One of many reasons I love the Pop-Up Debate tool is that it gives my students proof that they Belong in my class.

t: Negotiating With Team Members Looking to Leave
q: Beyond appealing to their loyalty to their colleagues and their place in the future of the team, leaders typically have several incentives at their disposal to retain a valued team member.
After this pattern repeats itself with several team members over time, leaders unintentionally create a terrorist mindset within the team.
Team members quickly learn that to get more, they must threaten to leave.
In the end, most team members with an offer will leave anyway, unless the bid to retain them is massive.
Counteroffer terrorism is created in organizations by leaders, not by team members.

t: Strengthening Weak Ties to the Organization
q: Over time, team members without a strong connection to the organization will slowly disconnect and fade away.
The question is not why a weak tie exists, but rather how leaders can strengthen the connection and reengage the commitment of any team member who seems less connected than their peers.
The best leaders insist team members with weak ties contribute to assignments that require full engagement, in many cases with multiple colleagues.
It is nearly impossible for a team member to maintain a weak connection to the team if the leader doesn’t allow it.
Not surprisingly, increasing the connection any team member has with the team depends on more frequent and substantive communication.

t: Leaders Who Lack Courage Allow Bad Ideas to Prosper
q: Exceptional leaders don’t make nearly as many good decisions as they do preventing bad ones from gaining traction.
The best leaders know that several good decisions can easily be wiped out by one bad one.
Taking away the oxygen a bad proposal needs to gain a foothold within the team requires the courage to hold a strong view and stick to it.
The best leaders even sniff around looking for poor decisions that have taken hold without much discussion.
Courageous leaders say “No” much more often than they say “Yes.

t: On Thinking Gray
q: Any time a leader oversimplifies a decision or issue by choosing to see things in extreme good’s and bad’s or right’s and wrong’s, they typically make poor choices and draw inadequate conclusions.
By giving up the middle ground, or shades of gray, leaders lose the flexibility to appreciate the complexity inherent in situations and people.
They care about understanding the factors at play that are obscure or lie underneath what is apparent on the face.
More specifically, thinking gray requires leaders to seek out strong and opposite opinions about an issue or experience.
Those who resist thinking gray do so at their own peril as decision-makers.

t: How to Get Through Your Curriculum This Year (Credibility Booster)
q: Schedules get disrupted, tangents get taken, rants get ranted, projects go over, and deadlines get shifted. Before you know it, you're weeks behind where you need to be to finish the curriculum.
And I'd also argue that it undermines our Credibility, which is both the most fundamental and the most controllable of the student motivation beliefs that exist in our classrooms.
Give me no deadline, and I'll write you a book when I get to it. Give me deadlines, and I may miss the first few, but I'll get that book out way before I would have had I not had any deadlines.
This helps me make mid-unit adjustments, like: Where can I speed things up if I'm short on time? Where can I linger if we've got extra time I hadn't planned on?
Now you'll know that you're not the problem, the curriculum is. And you can make or advocate for the adjustments that need to happen.
But until you use these two tools, I don't think it's accurate to point the finger at the curriculum.

t: How To Not Be Stressed Out This School Year https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2024/08/01/how-to-not-be-stressed-out-this-school-year/
q: Show me a stressed-out teacher and I’ll show you students bouncing off the walls. They go hand in hand like hot weather and mosquitos.
To avoid stress, you must allow your classroom management plan to do all of the dirty work of curbing misbehavior for you.
When you refuse to create friction with students (i.e. lecturing, questioning, berating, glaring, etc.), you remove a massive amount of stress.
Forcing yourself to meditate can bring on its own stress. All you really need to do is breathe through your nose and allow your exhales to linger.
To be at your even-keeled best, you have to get away from school. As soon as you leave the parking lot, shift your focus to family, friends, and hobbies.
